IN
THE COURT OF QUEEN’S BENCH OF NEW BRUNSWICK

TRIAL
DIVISION

JUDICIAL
DISTRICT OF MONCTON

MC/500/2017

Date: 2020/04/24

Citation No.: 2020 NBQB 083

BETWEEN:
Gordon
Wayne Bruce Hawkins

Plaintiff

-

and
–

Brian
Jamieson

Defendant

DECISION

BEFORE:                             Justice
Robert Dysart

AT:                                         Moncton,
New Brunswick

DATES
OF VOIR DIRE:    January 23 & February 21, 2020

DATE
OF DECISION:        April 24, 2020

APPEARANCES:               R.
Bruce Johnson, Esq. for the Plaintiff

Edwin G. Ehrhardt,
Q.C. for the Defendant

DYSART, J.

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]

The Plaintiff, Gordon Wayne Bruce Hawkins, is
suing his former business associate for alleged defamation. Mr. Hawkins, who
goes by the name David Hawkins, has been in the communications and advertising
business for over 40 years.

[
2
]

In 2011, Mr. Hawkins went into business with
the Defendant, Brian Jamieson, who was also involved in the communications and
advertising industry. They became shareholders in a closely-held company called
XYZ Stratégie-Communication Inc. (hereinafter “XYZ”).

[
3
]

In 2017, this business relationship came to
an end.  Ultimately, Mr. Hawkins and his wife purchased Mr. Jamieson’s shares
in XYZ. Unfortunately, the parties were unable to agree on a number of issues
pertaining to the sale of shares and the distribution of the company’s assets
and accounts receivable.  Mr. Jamieson maintains that Mr. Hawkins owed him a
share of the company’s receivables.

[
4
]

Shortly thereafter, Mr. Jamieson posted a
statement on his Facebook page, hypothetically referring to his unnamed business
partner. Mr. Hawkins alleges that the post was referring to him, and that it
was defamatory in nature. He seeks general damages, aggravated and punitive
damages as against Mr. Jamieson.

[
5
]

For his part, Mr. Jamieson maintains that the
Facebook post was essentially true, and therefore not defamatory. He pleads the
defence of justification.  He further claims that Mr. Hawkins has breached his
obligation to share the accounts receivable for XYZ, and he counterclaims for
those amounts and for other expenditures incurred by XYZ which Mr. Jamieson
alleges were, in reality, for the benefit of Mr. Hawkins personally.

BACKGROUND

[
6
]

In 2010, Mr. Hawkins caused to be
incorporated XYZ, a company he started with his wife Lorrie Bell-Hawkins.

[
7
]

In 2011, the Defendant, Brian Jamieson,
obtained a 50% ownership stake in XYZ. He held those shares through his own
company, 621947 NB Inc. (the “numbered company”), which was the actual
shareholder.  Both Mr. Hawkins and Mr. Jamieson had worked in the
communications and advertising business in the past, and from 2011 until 2016,
XYZ carried on business in a consistent fashion.

[
8
]

When the numbered company became a
shareholder in XYZ, the shareholders executed a Buy-Sell Agreement dated March
1, 2011 (also referred to by the parties as the “shotgun” agreement).
According to the provisions of that agreement, either shareholder could make an
offer to sell their shares to the other at an arbitrary price, i.e. not
necessarily linked to the value of the business (note: Mr. Hawkins and Ms.
Bell-Hawkins were considered a single shareholder under the Buy-Sell Agreement,
as were Mr. Jamieson and his numbered company).  The shareholder who received
such an offer could elect to either (a) sell their shares to the offering
shareholder at the offered price, or (b) purchase the offeror’s shares at the offered
price.

[
9
]

At all times, Ms. Bell-Hawkins was the
company’s sole employee, working as the administrator/bookkeeper. She was paid
$1,000 per month. XYZ paid all business expenses (rent, insurance, accounting
fees, etc.) from revenues. Net profits were paid to the shareholders in
accordance with their ownership stake, i.e. 50% was paid to Mr. Hawkins and Ms.
Bell-Hawkins, and 50% was paid to Mr. Jamieson’s numbered company.

[
10
]

The payments to the shareholders were done in
two ways: Mr. Hawkins and Mr. Jamieson, neither of whom was employed by XYZ,
routinely issued invoices to XYZ for professional services rendered to the
company; and, at various times and at the end of each year, retained earnings
were paid out on the same 50-50 basis to the shareholders as dividends.

[
11
]

Mr. Hawkins was the president of XYZ, as he
had been from its incorporation. Ms. Bell-Hawkins was XYZ’s Secretary-Treasurer.
The Court did not hear any evidence pertaining to other officers or directors
of the company, but it does not appear that Mr. Jamieson was ever a director or
officer of XYZ.

[
12
]

As president, Mr. Hawkins determined when
invoices were sent to clients; he also determined what charitable and strategic
donations were made by XYZ.

[
13
]

Based on the evidence before the Court, it
does not appear that Mr. Jamieson, as a shareholder (through the numbered
company) played any active role in the financial operations of the business.
That is not to say that he was not involved in business development or in
performing the actual work for XYZ’s clients, but he was not what might be
termed an “active” investor, overseeing each and every aspect of the business.
He left that, for the most part, to Mr. Hawkins.

THE BEGINNING OF THE END

[
14
]

In September 2016, Mr. Hawkins decided that
he would be leaving XYZ, and that presumably he and his wife would either sell
their shares to Mr. Jamieson or the company would be wound down.

[
15
]

On September 30, 2016, Mr. Hawkins sent an
email to Mr. Jamieson. That email addressed a number of issues pertaining to
XYZ, including its lease, ongoing projects, etc.  Regarding XYZ as a
corporation, that email read:

“XYZ as a company - my view is simple, we are best to end
XYZ as an operating company on December 31 – bury the brand - and find a
formula to split the very few assets. That said, the shareholders agreement is
in place and if either of us wants to pursue a different path - it can very
easily be dealt with just by exercising the shotgun clause.”

[
16
]

Later that month, on October 29, 2016, Mr.
Hawkins and Mr. Jamieson continued to discuss what to do with XYZ. In an email
of that date, Mr. Hawkins advised Mr. Jamieson that the company was showing
approximately $38,000 in retained earnings, all of which would be “bonused out
shortly.” In addition, Mr. Hawkins indicated that the company’s assets were
minimal, possibly $4,000 or less. He then writes: “The largest financial asset
is actually work in progress.”

[
17
]

By early January 2017, the parties still had
not reached any resolution as to whether to wind down XYZ or deal with the
shareholdings through a purchase and sale.

[
18
]

On January 2, 2017, Mr. Hawkins wrote to Mr.
Jamieson, outlining the options. He wrote:

“There are just three choices that I am aware of:

1.

Wrap
it up completely, cease operations and fold the company and brand - divide the
assets. We are actually quite close to that now with just 3-4 projects to
complete and not taking on any new ones.

2.

You
take the company and the brand.

3.

I
take the company and the brand.

While it does not seem practical, I suppose that a fourth
option might be to sell to a third party.”

[
19
]

In an email to Mr. Jamieson on January 3,
2017, Mr. Hawkins advised that XYZ could safely distribute its existing
retained earnings from 2016, which amounted to approximately $18,000 each. Mr.
Hawkins confirmed on cross-examination that, in fact, that money was
distributed later in January 2017.  Also, in that email, Mr. Hawkins advised
that he was arranging to pre-pay all anticipated expenses for XYZ through to
April 30, 2017, which included rent and anticipated accounting fees. Mr.
Hawkins was clear that the numbers were not final, writing “Please don’t hold
me to this…” but he then went on to estimate that the shareholders could likely
anticipate splitting a further $82,000 in additional revenue that would be
generated from work in progress. Recall that Mr. Hawkins had indicated that
work in progress was the company’s largest asset.

[
20
]

On January 15, 2017, Mr. Hawkins again wrote
to Mr. Jamieson by email, suggesting that there was, in his view, a “kind of
book of business” for XYZ in the nature of ongoing relationships and
reputation. He seemed to be describing goodwill, i.e. a value over and above
assets and accounts receivable. Mr. Hawkins advised that his valuation of his
and his wife’s shares in XYZ was $32,000. Obviously, given that Mr. Hawkins
felt that there was goodwill value in the brand, and given that accounts
receivable were anticipated to be worth upwards of $40,000 each, his analysis
of the value of his and his wife’s shares did not include those receivables.

[
21
]

On that same day, Mr. Jamieson wrote to Mr.
Hawkins. He wrote:

“With regard to your attachment to this email outlining
the assets of XYZ [which was not included in the evidence before the Court], I
don’t disagree with any of your assessment although frankly I feel that the
brand doesn’t really have much of any value to anyone other than me. There is
no book of business on the table and no contractual revenue at all.

In my view there are really only two things with any
transferable value - one is the XYZ brand itself and I don’t dispute that has
some value to me after six or so years in the market - as opposed to working as
Brian Jamieson, there is no question that it has a value to me and I’m willing
to pay for that at the right price.

The second is the transformation tool - I think you’ve said
a number of times that 1440s have accounted for 80% or more of the profit of
XYZ in recent years. The IP for the transformation tool is not something that
is on the table for sale in that I think it would be unlikely that anyone could
claim the ownership of that IP was ever acquired by XYZ - I have very detailed
notes of how and why that tool was created that predate the existence of XYZ.

Having said all of that, I very much want to continue
with the XYZ brand in exactly the way that I have envisioned since the start of
this relationship. And I very much hope we can find a way to make that happen.
So far, people are having very little difficulty seeing this as just a natural
progression of the business- I’d like to work hard to make sure we can find a
way to move forward and keep it that way.

Let me know when you think year-end numbers will be
available as well as any revenue continuing into 2017 and we’ll proceed from
there.”

[
22
]

It seems clear that, while there are
discussions over the value of the brand and the hard assets of the company, and
while there are discussions over who will purchase shares from whom, there is –
at least in the mind of Mr. Jamieson – an expectation that there will be
continued revenues and sharing of revenues into 2017 regardless of who
purchases the shares from whom.

[
23
]

On January 22, 2017, Mr. Jamieson wrote to
Mr. Hawkins as follows:

“Ok, let’s proceed on the assumption that I will buy your
shares at [$32,000] - since it looks like we’ll have receivables continuing to
come in for several months, perhaps we can arrange payment in a few instalments
between March and August or September if that doesn’t cause any undue
problems.  Would be very helpful to see the year end statements and AR aging
report as soon as they are available.”

[
24
]

Once again, this would indicate that Mr.
Jamieson is operating on the assumption that there would be a price paid for
the shares to represent the value of the brand and the limited number of
assets, but that the share value would not incorporate the accounts receivable,
which would continue to be split 50-50.

[
25
]

Later that same day, Mr. Hawkins responded.
He indicated that the revised estimates, based upon further invoicing and
receipts, was that the company would have approximately $115,500 in further
revenue, such that each shareholder could expect a distribution of $57,500.
Recall, this is at the same time that Mr. Hawkins is indicating that his shares
were worth $32,000, again suggesting that his share valuation excluded the
accounts receivable.

[
26
]

Later that same day, i.e. January 22, 2017,
Mr. Hawkins again writes to Mr. Jamieson.  He suggested that they select date
when the company would have sufficient funds to pay them $32,000 each.  They
would conclude the transaction for the sale of the shares on that date, with
Mr. Jamieson then assuming the accounts receivable and Mr. Hawkins invoicing
the company for his share.  That is, Mr. Hawkins is confirming the
understanding that, notwithstanding the sale of shares in XYZ, there would
continue to be an equal distribution of the accounts receivable as there had
been since the outset.

[
27
]

Throughout the month of February 2017,
discussions continued.  There was an agreement in principle reached, it would
seem, whereby Mr. Jamieson was to purchase Mr. Hawkins’ and Ms. Bell-Hawkins’ shares
for $32,000.  Mr. Jamieson then backed away from that, arguing that news of Mr.
Hawkins’ involvement with another communications and advertising firm had the
effect of reducing the value of the XYZ brand.  “[…] the brand is obviously no
longer worth $64k as we had agreed […]” he wrote.

[
28
]

On February 26, 2017, Mr. Hawkins
unilaterally instructed his legal counsel to begin the necessary steps to wind
down the company.  He indicated that Mr. Jamieson seemed unwilling to purchase
the Hawkins’ shares, and he, Mr. Hawkins, was not prepared to purchase Mr.
Jamieson’s.

[
29
]

Mr. Jamieson, in response, suggested that Mr.
Hawkins was acting disingenuously, which escalated the animosity as between the
two men.  Mr. Hawkins wrote a lengthy email to Mr. Jamieson on March 2, 2017.
In that email, he defended his valuation of his shares, going so far as to
suggest that he had obtained a valuation from the company’s accountants, Grant
Thornton, which indicated that the business was worth “[…] way, way over
$100,000 […] I clearly outlined the company assets as I saw them – and put
forward a valuation of 32k.”

[
30
]

Mr. Hawkins went on as follows:

“ […] in any case, XYZ clearly needs to transition – and
in light of the above (and below) – as far as I can see, there are now perhaps
just two viable options that I am aware of at this time – wind up the business
in a business-like way, as I have communicated in other e-mails over the past
few days.  Or you purchase them [i.e. the shares.]

If you no longer want to pay 32k – as I expressed above –
fine – that is your choice of course.  But, given the history of this – and
your idea that I am a disingenuous person… then the shotgun clause is the (sic)
by far the simplest, clearest, most efficient and most direct way to deal with
this matter.  In fact, that is pretty much the rationale for its existence.”

[
31
]

Mr. Hawkins advised that all further
communications should be directed to his legal counsel (who had, in fact, been
acting as counsel to the company for many years).

[
32
]

On March 6, 2017, Mr. Hawkins again wrote to
Mr. Jamieson.  He advised that their working relationship was badly damaged.
He wrote: “So, what’s left?” and then documented the status of various projects
and accounts.  He stated that two of those projects would be completed and
invoiced by the end of that week with another anticipated to be invoiced by the
end of March.  He wrote:

“There will be substantial [accounts receivable] coming
in over the next few weeks.  As always, we will pay out all [accounts payable]
and split the remaining funds 50/50, as usual.”

[
33
]

Mr. Hawkins anticipated that, even if they
were unable to collect on one of the accounts, their share was likely in the
range of $40,000 each.

“Following that [i.e. the payout], unless something new
or different surfaces, the company will probably go into neutral indefinitely.
… As I have expressed in the past, if you want to purchase our shares, simply put
forward an offer.  It need not be in the shotgun format, but it will need to be
clear.  If you do not plan to do that, fine.  Please indicate that in a timely
way as well.”

[
34
]

Again, the value of the shares as proposed by
Mr. Hawkins was less than half the anticipated receivables, such that the only
reasonable conclusion was that the parties continued to operate on the understanding
that, notwithstanding the sale of shares, there would be a 50-50 distribution
of the profits, i.e. that the receivables would not be included in any deal for
the sale of the shares.

THE BUY-SELL AGREEMENT

[
35
]

A few days later, on March 11, 2017, Mr.
Jamieson triggered the Buy-Sell Agreement by making an offer to sell his
company’s shares in XYZ to Mr. Hawkins and Ms. Bell-Hawkins for the price of
$10,000.  In accordance with the terms of the Buy-Sell Agreement, they had the
option of either accepting the offer or requiring Mr. Jamieson to purchase
their shares at that same price.  They agreed to purchase Mr. Jamieson’s
shares.  The acceptance was served on Mr. Jamieson on March 31, 2017.  The
closing date was set for May 1, 2017.

[
36
]

That same evening, i.e. March 31, 2017, Mr. Jamieson
reached out to Mr. Hawkins by text message, asking: “Is there anything now
preventing the cash flow of XYZ from being disbursed to shareholders
immediately?”  Mr. Hawkins replied the following day, advising that “there were
a number of important reasons as to why we did not accept your offer.  We will
be back on the 17
th
.  Perhaps it will be a good idea to review this
matter at that time.”

[
37
]

On the next day, April 2, 2017, there is
another exchange.  Mr. Jamieson wrote: “So you continue to refuse to release
the receivables.  Unless I have confirmation that a cheque has been dropped off
at the office today, we’ll proceed to the next stage Monday morning.”  There
was no evidence before the Court to explain what Mr. Jamieson was referring to
as “the next stage,” but it is clear that Mr. Jamieson expected to receive 50%
share of the receivables, notwithstanding that the so-called shotgun clause had
been triggered.

[
38
]

In response, Mr. Hawkins wrote:

“Brian – As mentioned above, we are away for a few days
shortly (sic) but back on the 17
th
.  If, at that time, you wish to
talk about an offer that would – in my view – work well for all parties, we can
talk about that during that week.”

[
39
]

In his affidavit sworn on November 30, 2017,
Mr. Hawkins indicates, in relation to that email to Mr. Jamieson, that he was
“fully prepared to discuss an alternate proposal that would work well for all
parties upon my return.”

[
40
]

That same day, i.e. April 2, 2017, Mr.
Hawkins wrote to Mr. Jamieson and advised:

“The facts are these – XYZ has some receivables – not a
lot – and a relatively small amount of cash, much of which it is likely to
need.  But there are a few other reasons which Bruce Johnson will make very
clear.”

[
41
]

No further explanation was provided for what
Mr. Hawkins meant by “other reasons” – but it seems that, for the first time,
Mr. Hawkins is rejecting the notion of an equal division of profits, and that ,
notwithstanding his advice only one month earlier that they could each
anticipate receiving $40,000 in profit distributions, Mr. Hawkins did not
intend to allow XYZ to make any distribution to the shareholders.

[
42
]

There were some further discussions as
between the parties in mid-April 2017, but it would seem those discussions were
without prejudice, as neither party provided particulars.  It is clear that Mr.
Hawkins’ counsel invited counsel for Mr. Jamieson to engage in discussions
regarding Mr. Jamieson’s expectations on several occasions, but Mr. Jamieson
refused those invitations.

[
43
]

In the days leading to May 1, 2017, Mr.
Jamieson instructed his counsel not to proceed with the closing.  The reason
for that refusal was first articulated in correspondence dated May 9, 2017 (at
least, that is the first document in evidence which addresses the issue).  At
that time, counsel for Mr. Jamieson advised that her client had refused to
proceed with the closing on the basis that he did not receive adequate
financial disclosure regarding XYZ’s operations for the period January to April
2017.  As a result, the letter states, Mr. Jamieson was unable to determine the
precise amount of money owed to him by XYZ – presumably his 50% share of the
net receivables.

[
44
]

In response, counsel for Mr. Hawkins
responded by email, writing:

“On the closing date of May 1, 2017, I am advised that
there was no indebtedness owing by the Corporation to the Vendor recorded on
the books of the Corporation and therefore no monies payable pursuant to
paragraph 8(b) of the Buy-Sell Agreement on closing.”

[
45
]

Counsel for Mr. Hawkins also asked for the
copies of emails from Mr. Hawkins which purportedly supported the claim for
those amounts.  There is no evidence to suggest that such emails were ever
provided by Mr. Jamieson or his lawyers.

[
46
]

The Buy-Sell Agreement provided that, should
the selling party fair or refuse to proceed with the closing, the purchaser was
designated as the seller’s attorney.  That is, because Mr. Jamieson refused to
provide the necessary signed paperwork to complete the closing, Mr. Hawkins and
Ms. Bell-Hawkins executed that paperwork on his behalf and proceeded with the
closing despite the objections of Mr. Jamieson’s counsel.

[
47
]

In an email dated June 2, 2017, counsel for
Mr. Hawkins advised Mr. Jamieson’s lawyers as follows:

“Your clients, without notice, elected to exercise their
rights under the Buy-Sell Agreement dated March 1, 2011 (the “Buy-Sell
Agreement”);

Your clients presented a
bare bones shotgun offer dated March 27, 2017 (the “Shotgun Offer”) which
failed to address any of the normal provisions that one would find in a share
purchase agreement;

The Shotgun Offer only made reference to the purchase
price and a closing date;

The Shotgun Offer did not address any other obligations
of any of the parties either pre or post-closing and specifically did not
provide for any assets to be distributed to the shareholders of XYZ or
otherwise; …

The terms were exactly the same for each side of the
transaction i.e. if our clients had elected to sell their shares, they would
not be entitled to anything more, as a shareholder, than the purchase price set
forth in the Shotgun Offer;

The parties entered into a binding contract which defined
the go forward relationship of the parties in respect of their interests and
rights as shareholders […]”

[
48
]

Mr. Hawkins, notwithstanding the practice of
sharing the net profits on a 50-50 basis, considered that the Buy-Sell
Agreement displaced the long-standing practice and entitled him (and his wife),
as the Purchaser of the shares, to keep all net profits.  To be precise, as set
out at paragraph 63 of his affidavit sworn on November 30, 2017, Mr. Hawkins
took the position that the Corporation was not formally indebted to Mr.
Jamieson, and so no amount was payable.

[
49
]

The evidence is that certain of the invoices
which were supposed to have been sent to XYZ’s clients by late March 2017, in
fact, were not.  Mr. Hawkins testified that at least one of the ongoing projects
which Mr. Jamieson was completing, was not invoiced until approximately May
2017 – i.e. after the closing.  In addition, the project which Mr. Hawkins
expected to have billed by in early March was not completed until the summer.
At trial, he testified that he spent upwards of 290 hours to complete that
project after the closing, and that the invoice was not sent to the client
until October 2017 – which invoice was in the amount of $59,000.  That is, Mr.
Hawkins continued to operate XYZ until at least October.

[
50
]

Ultimately, Mr. Jamieson did not receive any
further amounts after the dividends were paid out in early January 2017.
Further, he was not paid the $10,000 for his shares, apparently because he did
not provide the required closing documents.

THE FACEBOOK POSTING

[
51
]

On June 21, 2017, Mr. Jamieson wrote a
Facebook posting on his wall.  The posting read as follows:

“Hypothetically, if you caught your 50/50 business
partner stealing from the company, acknowledging it in writing, refusing to
either correct it or apologize, doing it again, and then walking off with a
hundred grand in receivables, sooner or later you’d say, enough is enough,
right?  I think sometimes a bully just needs to be called out.  Hypothetically,
of course.”

[
52
]

According to Mr. Hawkins’ affidavit, the
posting was removed the next day.

[
53
]

The uncontroverted evidence is that, at the
time, Mr. Jamieson had approximately 600 Facebook “friends,” many of whom were
other members of the communications and advertising community, and many of whom
were clients and so-called “key individuals,” i.e. politicians and persons in
leadership positions in industry.  That said, despite Mr. Hawkins’ bare
assertion in his affidavit evidence that the posting was broadly disseminated
throughout North America, there was no evidence before the Court pertaining to
the number of people who may have read the post, nor was there any evidence as
to whether the post was shared and disseminated to others.

[
54
]

Demands for an apology and a public
retraction were refused by Mr. Jamieson.

[
55
]

In May 2018, Mr. Jamieson apparently sent a
text message to his ex-wife in which he wrote: “I no longer have a business
partner stealing from the company bank account.”  Neither a copy of that text
message was not produced, nor did the recipient provide an affidavit.

LITIGATION

[
56
]

Mr. Hawkins commenced this action on July 5,
2017.  He claims damages in defamation, including general damages, aggravated
damages and punitive damages.

[
57
]

On August 4, 2017, Mr. Jamieson filed a
Statement of Defence and Counterclaim.  Mr. Jamieson asserts a defence of
justification, maintaining that the Facebook posting was essentially true.  He
further claims that Mr. Hawkins is liable to him for various amounts owed to
him by XYZ, including his 50% share of the company’s net profits, an amount
representing 50% of certain charitable donations made in the final three months
of 2016; and an amount representing 50% of the value of a membership purchased
by Mr. Hawkins in a social club, which shares were paid for by XYZ.

[
58
]

The action was commended under rule 79 of the
rules of Court.  No examinations for discovery took place.  Affidavits were
admitted by consent.  Only Mr. Hawkins was cross-examined at trial.

ISSUES

[
59
]

The issues to be determined are as follows:

1.

Did
the Facebook posting by Mr. Jamieson constitute defamation?

2.

If
so, is there an available defence of justification?

3.

If
there is no defence, what are the appropriate general damages?  Is Mr. Hawkins entitled
to aggravated damages and/or punitive damages?

4.

As
for the counterclaim, is Jamieson entitled to any damages as against Mr.
Hawkins?  If so, what are those damages?

EVIDENCE

[
60
]

As stated, this action was commenced pursuant
to the Simplified Procedure Rule, i.e. Rule 79 of he Rules of Court.  As such,
the vast majority of the evidence was tendered by affidavit.

[
61
]

The affidavit evidence before the Court (all
entered by consent of the parties) was as follows:

For the Plaintiff:

1.

Affidavit of David Hawkins sworn on November
30, 2017;

2.

Affidavit of David Hawkins sworn on May 24,
2018;

3.

Affidavit of David Hawkins sworn on July 4,
2018;

4.

Affidavit of Frederic Gionet sworn on
November 30, 2017;

5.

Affidavit of Catherine Manuel sworn on
November 30, 2017;

6.

Affidavit of Brian Cormier sworn on November
30, 2017; and

7.

Affidavit of Paul F. Bradley sworn on June 4,
2018.

For the Defendant:

1.

Affidavit of Brian Jamieson sworn on March
21, 2018; and

2.

Affidavit of Brian Jamieson sworn on October
15, 2018.

Affidavits of Frederic Gionet, Catherine
Manuel and Brian Cormier

[
62
]

Each of the above affiants was a Facebook
“friend” of Mr. Jamieson’s in June 2017.  Each has sworn that he or she read
the Facebook post and each has sworn that he or she concluded that the post was
referring to Mr. Hawkins as the “50/50 business partner.”

Affidavit and Report of Paul F. Bradley,
Expert

[
63
]

Mr. Bradley’s affidavit attaches as an
exhibit a report which was prepared under his supervision which is dated May
29, 2018.  That report, titled a “Valuation Report,” purports to calculate the
value of XYZ as a business effective April 30, 2017, i.e. the day preceding the
closing of the sale of shares.

[
64
]

Mr. Bradley is partner with Deloitte LLP.
With Mr. Jamieson’s consent, he was declared an expert in business valuations
and his report was admitted into evidence.

[
65
]

Mr. Bradley prepared his report at the
request of Mr. Hawkins’ counsel.  At the outset of the report, he advises that
the report was prepared on the basis of “minimal” review or analysis of XYZ’s
records, and with “little or no corroboration of relevant information.”  Mr.
Bradley opines that, after considering XYZ’s assets, its potential liabilities

[

]

At the outset of the hearing in this matter,
it was expressly stated and understood that the Facebook post referenced two

1.

That he stole from the company; and

2.

That he “walked off” with $100,000 in

[

It was further clarified that, with respect

THE LEGAL ELEMENTS OF DEFAMATION

[
75
]

In terms of what type of communication
amounts to actionable defamation, the Plaintiff relies on the Supreme Court of
Canada decision of
Grant v. Torstar Corp
.,
2009 SCC 61 (CanLII)
,
where the Court held:

[28]
A plaintiff in a defamation action is
required to prove three things to obtain  judgment and an award of damages: (1)
that the impugned words were defamatory, in the sense that they would tend to
lower the plaintiff’s reputation in the eyes of a reasonable person; (2) that
the words in fact referred to the plaintiff; and (3) that the words were
published
, meaning that they were communicated to at least one person other
than the plaintiff.  If these elements are established on a balance of probabilities,
falsity and damage are presumed, though this rule has been subject to strong
criticism: see, e.g., R. A. Smolla, “Balancing Freedom of Expression and
Protection of Reputation Under Canada’s Charter of Rights and Freedoms”, in D.
Schneiderman, ed., Freedom of Expression and the
Charter
(1991), 272, at p.
282. (The only exception is that slander requires proof of special damages,
unless the impugned words were slanderous per se:  R. E. Brown, The Law of
Defamation in Canada (2nd ed. (loose-leaf)), vol. 3, at pp. 25-2 and 25-3.) The
plaintiff is not required to show that the defendant intended to do harm, or
even that the defendant was careless. The tort is thus one of strict liability.

[29] If the plaintiff proves the required elements, the
onus then shifts to the defendant to advance a defence in order to escape
liability.

[emphasis
added]

DID THE WORDS USED REFER TO THE
PLAINTIFF?

[
76
]

Taking the elements slightly out of order, I
will first address the question of whether the Facebook post, which did not
identify the “50/50 business partner” by name, referred to David Hawkins.

[
77
]

Firstly, it should be stated that Mr.
Jamieson does not deny that he was referring to Mr. Hawkins.  He was.  But the
issue that must be determined by the Court is whether a reader of the post
would likely identify the business partner as Mr. Hawkins.

[
78
]

The Plaintiff cites
Grant v.
Cormier-Grant
,
2001 CanLII 3041 (ON CA)
, where the Ontario Court of
Appeal held that the test is whether the words would reasonably lead a person
or persons acquainted with the Plaintiff to believe that he or she is the
person referred to.

[
79
]

In this case, the Court has evidence from
three persons, all acquaintances of Mr. Hawkins, all of whom immediately
concluded that Mr. Jamieson’s post was referring to David Hawkins.

[
80
]

I am satisfied that, even if Mr. Hawkins was
not personally named in the post, he was sufficiently identified so as to give
rise to an action in defamation.  The second element of the tort is therefore
met.

WERE THE IMPUGNED WORDS DEFEMATORY?

[
81
]

In
Botiuk v. Toronto Free Press
Publications Ltd.
,
1995 CanLII 60 (SCC)
, the Supreme Court stated:

[62]               For the purposes of these reasons, it
is sufficient to observe that a publication which tends to lower a person in
the estimation of right
‑
thinking members of
society, or to expose a person to hatred, contempt or ridicule, is defamatory
and will attract liability.  See
Cherneskey v. Armadale Publishers Ltd
.,

1978 CanLII 20 (SCC)
,
[1979] 1 S.C.R. 1067
, at p. 1079
.  What is defamatory may
be determined from the ordinary meaning of the published words themselves or
from the surrounding circumstances.  In
The Law of Defamation in Canada

(2nd ed. 1994), R. E. Brown stated the following at p. 1
‑
15:

[A publication] may be defamatory in its plain and
ordinary meaning or by virtue of extrinsic facts or circumstances, known to the
listener or reader, which give it a defamatory meaning by way of innuendo
different from that in which it ordinarily would be understood.  In determining
its meaning, the court may take into consideration all the circumstances of the
case, including any reasonable implications the words may bear, the context in
which the words are used, the audience to whom they were published and the
manner in which they were presented.

[
82
]

Did the Facebook in this case “tend to lower
a person in the minds of right-thinking individuals?’  The answer is, yes.  Mr.
Jamieson suggests that his business partner stole from the company.  Stealing
is a criminal offence, and there can be no doubt that such an allegation has
the impact of tarnishing the reputation and integrity of the person against
whom it is made. The post made Mr. Hawkins out to be someone who acted
dishonestly.

[
83
]

Further, the reference to Mr. Hawkins
“walking off with a hundred grand” implies that he did so without colour of
right, again implying, at the very least, unlawful (as opposed to criminal) conduct.

[
84
]

In
Mueller v Livingstone
,
2019
NBQB 28 (CanLII)
, Justice Clendening of this Court considered a case involving
allegations of defamation.  The plaintiff, the owner of an art gallery, got
into a dispute with one of the artists with whom she had a contract.  The
relationship soured, and the artist made a post to Facebook, suggesting that
the Plaintiff had committed theft.  Justice Clendening wrote:

[19]      […] The plaintiff argues
that by using the word “theft” the defendant has characterized the plaintiff as
a person who walked away with the money permanently stolen, and it was not just
mere indebtedness, but reached the level of criminality.

[20]      Mr. Justice Morrison
stated
in
Jones v Barton
,
2014 NBQB 42
, words must be construed in their
ordinary meaning.  At paragraph 19 he indicated that the test is “fair and
actual meaning given to words by a reasonable person of ordinary intelligence”.
The words in the matter before me are clear and unambiguous and reach the level
of defamation.

[
85
]

In my view, suggesting that Mr. Hawkins stole
from XYZ amounts to defamation.

WERE THE WORDS PUBLISHED?

[
86
]

There can be little doubt that Mr. Jamieson’s
Facebook post to some 600 of his “friends” was a communication which meets the
requirements for a publication.
See
Mueller v. Livingstone
,
supra., where Justice Clendening wrote:

The third condition, that the words were published, is
established if it is accepted that Facebook posts indeed are a form of
publication,  and communicated to at least one person.  In this matter it is
known that at least 14 people shared the post and 33 people “liked it”.  There
were many comments made about the post suggesting that Ms. Mueller swindled Mr.
Livingstone and that she is a stinking crook.  Consequently, I find that the
Facebook post was published and it is evident that more than one person
received the publication.  Consequently, all three conditions are met as
described in
Grant v Torstar
, supra.  Being called a thief does not
include a person who avoids paying debts.  I find the words used by Mr.
Livingstone regarding the putting of money in one’s pocket being equated to
theft is defamatory.

[
87
]

In the present case, there is evidence that
many of Mr. Jamieson’s Facebook friends read the post.  Some commented on the
post by responding with a Facebook reaction, i.e. an angry face or similar
emoji character.  Some expressly made comments.

[
88
]

The post was a publication.

[
89
]

As a result, it is my finding that Mr.
Jamieson’s post was defamatory.

TRUTH AS A DEFENCE

[
90
]

Mr. Jamieson pleads the defence of
justification.  That is, while acknowledging that he posted the comments to his
Facebook page, he argues that the facts asserted in the post are substantially
true, and that truth is a defence to an action in defamation.  As stated by the
Supreme Court of Canada in
Grant v. Torstar
,
supra
:

[33] To succeed on the defence of justification, a
defendant must adduce evidence showing that the statement was substantially
true.

[
91
]

In
Jones v Barton
,
2014 NBQB 42
(CanLII)
, Justice Morrison of this Court reiterated the nature of the defence,
and cited from R. E. Brown,
The Law of Defamation in Canada
, a
leading text relating to defamation:

52.       The test for justification is set out in Brown,
supra, at page 513-515:

The defence of justification will succeed if the
defendant proves the truth of “every injurious imputation which the jury find
to be conveyed by the publication”.  In determining this issue, regard may be
had for the setting, context and circumstances in which the words were used.
It is the truth as the words would be reasonably understood in light of the
particular circumstances that must be proved.  Where the defamatory words are
couched in the form of statements of fact and expressions of opinions, the
defendant must prove that both are correct, unless of course a defence of fair
comment is available.  If the opinions, however, do not alter or change the
principal thrust or sting of the defamatory comments, they will not defeat the
defense of justification if the principal sting of the libel or slander is
shown to be true.

The evidence supporting the justification must be as
broad as the defamatory imputation.  However, it is not necessary to prove the
literal truth or “the truth of every fact” in the publication, if the
additional facts do not constitute a separate defamatory imputation, and the
justification otherwise meets the gist or sting of the charge.  Substantial
truth is the test.  The defendant must establish only that “the whole of the
defamatory matter is substantially true”.  It is the “sting” of the words that
the defendant must justify [...]

[
92
]

In
Ross v. Beutel
,
2001 NBCA 62
(CanLII)
, our Court of Appeal considered a case involving a political
cartoonist who had depicted the plaintiff, a school teacher who had published
books regarding an alleged Jewish international conspiracy, as a Nazi.  The
depiction was presented at a conference.  The Court of Appeal, in addressing
the defence of justification, wrote as follows:

“[80] […] In my view, the trial judge erred by requiring
that Beutel prove the comment made in the Goebbels cartoon to be true rather
than the facts upon which he relied in making the comment. The law is well
settled that Beutel need only prove the truth of the facts on which he relied
in making his comment: that is, a sufficient substratum of fact to warrant his
comment in the sense that a fair-minded person might on those facts honestly
hold that opinion.”

[
93
]

So, it would seem that, in order for Mr.
Jamieson’s defence of justification to be successful, he must prove, on the
balance of probabilities, that the facts which underlie his comments are
substantially true.  If he meets that burden, the defence is made.

[
94
]

Let us now consider each of the component
parts of the Facebook post to determine whether there is “a sufficient
substratum of fact to warrant his comment.”

[
95
]

As stated, the reference to Mr. Jamieson’s

ALLEGED THEFT – THE CHARITABLE DONATIONS

[

Each year between 2011 and 2016, XYZ made a

2011 - $4560

2012 - $13,625

2013 - $15,608

2014 - $22,500

2015 - $21,003

2016 - $35,015

As

[

In

[
100
]

Mr.
Hawkins testified during cross-examination that many of the donations were

]

]

MEMBERSHIP

[

or about 2013, Mr. Hawkins purchased a $2,000 membership in the Alma Club, a

There was no effort to hide the purchase – it was known to Mr. Jamieson for

]

Again,
Mr. Jamieson has not proven any underlying facts which could support his

[
107
]

The
defence of justification therefore fails as it pertains to the allegation of

ALLEDGEDLY “WALKING AWAY” WITH ACCOUNTS
RECEIVABLE

[
108
]

As
noted, Mr. Jamieson claimed that his business partner had stolen from the
company,
and
that he “walked away with a hundred grand in
receivables.”

[
109
]

Mr.
Jamieson again claims the defence of justification.  He maintains that Mr.
Hawkins, in refusing to divide XYZ’s net profits on a 50-50 basis, either
before the closing date for the sale of the shares or afterwards, amounted to a
breach of the long-standing agreement outlined above.

[
110
]

For
his part, Mr. Hawkins maintains that, once the Buy-Sell Agreement was
triggered, all former agreements or understandings came to an end.  He
maintains that that the Buy-Sell Agreement was a self-contained contract,

Jamieson) which was registered on the company’s books, there was nothing
payable other than the sale price, i.e. $10,000.

[
111
]

But
Mr. Hawkins’ position is in inconsistent with his own testimony as set out in
paragraph 40 of his affidavit sworn on November 30, 2017, which reads:

“Accordingly, we elected to accept the Defendant’s
Shotgun Offer and purchase the 50% ownership of 621947 N.B. Ltd. in the
Corporation with the hope that the Defendant and I could later work something
out that would enable him to acquire the Corporation’s brand that he had
expressed interest in acquiring, and for an equitable distribution of the
future net profits of the corporation, when determined.”

[
112
]

That
is, even after the Buy-Sell Agreement was triggered, Mr. Hawkins considered
that there should be an “equitable distribution” of XYZ’s net profits.

[
113
]

That
statement is in stark contrast with, and is completely incompatible with, the
position taken by Mr. Hawkins at paragraph 12 of his subsequent affidavit sworn

discussions and understandings as between the parties were effectively
extinguished once the Buy-Sell Agreement was triggered by Mr. Jamieson.

[
114
]

Was

Buy-Sell would set aside the prior agreement to share profits?

[
115
]

Mr.
Jamieson
cites
Bhasin v. Hrynew
,
2014 SCC 71 (CanLII)
, where the
Supreme Court of Canada confirmed the existence of a duty of good faith in the
context of contractual dealings.  Writing for the Court, Justice Cromwell
stated:

[60]                          Commercial parties
reasonably expect a basic level of honesty and good faith in contractual
dealings. While they remain at arm’s length and are not subject to the duties
of a fiduciary, a basic level of honest conduct is necessary to the proper
functioning of commerce. The growth of longer term, relational contracts that
depend on an element of trust and cooperation clearly call for a basic element
of honesty in performance, but, even in transactional exchanges, misleading or
deceitful conduct will fly in the face of the expectations of the parties: see Swan
and Adamski, at §1.24.

[...]

[65]                          The organizing principle of
good faith exemplifies the notion that, in carrying out his or her own
performance of the contract, a contracting party should have appropriate regard
to the legitimate contractual interests of the contracting partner. While
“appropriate regard” for the other party’s interests will vary depending on the
context of the contractual relationship, it does not require acting to serve
those interests in all cases. It merely requires that a party not seek to
undermine those interests in bad faith. This general principle has strong
conceptual differences from the much higher obligations of a fiduciary.  Unlike
fiduciary duties, good faith performance does not engage duties of loyalty to
the other contracting party or a duty to put the interests of the other
contracting party first.

[…]

[69]                          The approach of recognizing
an overarching organizing principle but accepting the existing law as the
primary guide to future development is appropriate in the development of the
doctrine of good faith. Good faith may be invoked in widely varying contexts
and this calls for a highly context-specific understanding of what honesty and
reasonableness in performance require so as to give appropriate consideration
to the legitimate interests of both contracting parties. For example, the
general organizing principle of good faith would likely have different
implications in the context of a long-term contract of mutual cooperation than
it would in a more transactional exchange: Swan and Adamski, at § 1.24; B.
Dixon, “Common law obligations of good faith in Australian commercial contracts
— a relational recipe” (2005), 33 A.B.L.R. 87.

[
116
]

Mr.
Jamieson maintains that, by not issuing any invoices from XYZ until after the
May 1
st
closing date, and by treating the Buy-Sell Agreement as the
sole contract as between the parties relating to XYZ, Mr. Hawkins has acted in
bad faith.

[
117
]

Further,
why did Mr. Hawkins not advise that there would be delays in issuing the
invoices? And why was there no disclosure of any records to substantiate Mr.
Hawkins’ claim of having worked another 290 hours after May 1
st
?

[
118
]

Why,
Mr. Jamieson asks, did Mr. Hawkins not expressly advise Mr. Jamieson after
March 31, 2017 that he would not be entitled to any receivables, having
exercised the Buy-Sell Agreement?

[
119
]

Mr.
Hawkins maintains that any earlier agreement, understanding or arrangement
relating to the distribution of profits was extinguished by the Buy-Sell Agreement,
which provides only that the selling shareholder is entitled to the sale price
and the repayment of any debts owed by XYZ which are registered on the
company’s books.  He maintains that XYZ would have paid any such debts, had
they been proven.

[
120
]

Of
course, Mr. Hawkins’ position is only valid if one accepts that the Buy-Sell
Agreement automatically extinguished the earlier arrangement. But on what basis
does Mr. Hawkins maintain that the earlier agreement was extinguished?  There
is no so-called “Entire Agreement” clause in the Buy-Sell Agreement, which one
often sees in such commercial contracts.  Such clauses would typically provide
that there are no prior representations, warranties or collateral agreements
other than what is expressly stated in the new agreement.

[
121
]

Here,
however, the Buy-Sell Agreement is silent in terms of the payment of net
profits and it does not contain an “Entire Agreement” clause.  In fact, Mr.
Hawkins’ own counsel acknowledges as much when he wrote on June 2, 2017:

Your clients presented a bare bones shotgun offer dated
March 27, 2017 (the “Shotgun Offer”) which failed to address any of the normal
provisions that one would find in a share purchase agreement;

The Shotgun Offer only made reference to the purchase
price and a closing date;

The Shotgun Offer did not address any other obligations
of any of the parties either pre or post-closing and specifically did not
provide for any assets to be distributed to the shareholders of XYZ or
otherwise; […]

[
122
]

If
the Buy-Sell Agreement did not contain an “Entire Agreement” clause, and if it
failed to address any issues pertaining to the assets to be distributed to the
shareholders, how can it be said that it extinguished the earlier agreement?

[
123
]

In
his pre-trial brief, Mr. Hawkins argues that the wording of the Buy-Sell
Agreement is clear, and that the Court should not consider any extrinsic
evidence pertaining to discussions or agreements between the parties which
pre-date the triggering of the shotgun offer.  Effectively, Mr. Hawkins argues
the parol evidence rule.  Mr. Jamieson argues that there was a separate and
distinct collateral contract.

[
124
]

The
issue of a collateral contract or agreement, separate but equally valid to the
contract at issue, was
considered by the Ontario Superior Court in
Michta
v Stewart
,
2016 ONSC 5989 (CanLII)
, where the Court wrote:

[18]           The nature of the parol evidence rule, and
of one of its exceptions, were described by the Court of Appeal in
Guttierrez
v. Tropic International Limited et al.

(2002),
2002 CanLII 45017 (ON CA)
,

63 O.R. (3d) 63
, at para.
19
. In that case, the court held that under the parol
evidence rule, when the language of a written contract is clear and
unambiguous, extrinsic evidence is not admissible to vary, qualify, add to, or
subtract from, the words of the written contract. However, the court went on to
say that the rule is not absolute, and admits of numerous exceptions: one of
those exceptions being cases where there is evidence of a distinct collateral
agreement, which does not contradict, and is not inconsistent with, the written
contract.

[
125
]

In
this case, Mr. Jamieson is not trying to invalidate or vary the terms of the Buy-Sell
Agreement; rather, he is arguing that there was another agreement, collateral
to the Buy-Sell Agreement and not inconsistent with it, which formed part of the
overall agreement between the parties.

[
126
]

In
my view, there is nothing which is inconsistent between the terms and
conditions of the Buy-Sell Agreement, which addresses the mechanism by which
the shares of XYZ may be sold and what documents and amounts are payable to the
selling shareholder at the date of closing, and the long-standing agreement,
which was repeatedly acknowledged and confirmed by Mr. Hawkins, that XYZ’s net
profits would be shared – even after the sale of shares had taken place.

[
127
]

Based
on the evidence before me, it is my finding that Mr. Hawkins did not act in
good faith in his contractual dealings with Mr. Jamieson following the
triggering of the Buy-Sell Agreement in late March 2017.  It is my conclusion
that Mr. Hawkins knew or ought to have known that the offer of $10,000 for the
shares did not include or in any way vary the agreement to share the
receivables.  Recall that only a few weeks earlier, Mr. Hawkins stated that the
receivables were worth upwards of $40,000 each.

[
128
]

It
is noteworthy that within 48 hours of accepting to purchase Mr. Jamieson’s
shares, Mr. Hawkins – for the very first time – suggested that there would be
“very little” cash to distribute.

[
129
]

Further,
it is my finding that Mr. Hawkins’ explanation for the delay in issuing invoices
until after May 1
st
, 2017 is unsatisfactory.  Why, if there was
going to be such a delay in issuing the invoices beyond the second week of
March 2017, did Mr. Hawkins not advise Mr. Jamieson?

[
130
]

Having
dragged those invoices past May 1
st
, Mr. Hawkins then attempted to
justify his actions by arguing the value of the shares was nil, which he knew
to be incorrect.  In fact, in his pleadings, Mr. Hawkins alleges that the
Facebook posting in late June 2017 had a serious detrimental effect on the
value of his shares.  So, which is it?  Why did he attempt to argue that the
shares were worth nothing as of the date of the closing?  He did not act in
good faith, in my view.

[
131
]

I
am satisfied that there is substantial truth to the underlying facts to
conclude that Mr. Hawkins “walked away” with the receivables which he was not
legally entitled to keep.

[
132
]

The
defence of justification is therefore met in respect to that portion of the
Facebook post.

GENERAL DAMAGES

[
133
]

Where
I have concluded that Mr. Jamieson is liable in defamation for having published
that Mr. Hawkins stole from the company, Mr. Hawkins is entitled to damages.

[
134
]

The
starting point is
section 2
of the
Defamation Act,
R.S.N.B. 2011,
c.139, which provides:

An action lies for defamation, and if defamation is
proved in an action for defamation, damage shall be presumed.

[
135
]

That
is, there is no obligation on the Plaintiff to prove actual damage to his
reputation in order to recover.

[
136
]

As
is often stated, damages in defamation, which cannot be calculated with
precision, are “damages at large,” with no cap on the amount of damages
available to a plaintiff (see
Hill v. Church of Scientology of Toronto
,

1995 CanLII 59 (SCC)
).

[
137
]

The
Plaintiff relies on a list of factors to be considered by the Court in
assessing general damages, as set out in the decision of
Leenen v.
Canadian Broadcasting Corp
.,
2000 CanLII 22380 (ON SC)
:

(a)
the seriousness of the defamatory statement;

(b)
the identity of the accuser;

(c)
the breadth of the distribution of the publication of the libel;

(d)
republication of the libel;

(e)
the failure to give the audience both sides of the picture and not presenting a
balanced review;

(f)
the desire to increase one's professional reputation or to increase ratings of
a particular program;

(g)
the conduct of the defendant and defendant's counsel through to the end of
trial;

(h)
the absence or refusal of any retraction or apology;

(i)
the failure to establish a plea of justification.

[
138
]

Ultimately,
Mr. Hawkins seeks general damages in the range of $50,000.  He cites a number
of cases,
including:
Nassri v. Homsi
,
2017 ONSC 4554 (CanLII)
;
Pinsent
v. Sandstrom
,
2014 ABQB 269 (CanLII)
;
Finocchio v. Kurtesi
,

[2007] O.J. No. 5581
;
Pritchard v. Van Nes
,
2016 BCSC 686
(CanLII)
; and
Jones v Barton
,
2014 NBQB 42 (CanLII)
.

[
139
]

For
his part, Mr. Jamieson suggests something at the much lower end of the
spectrum.  He cites the cases of
White v. Zed
,
2018 NBQB 176
(CanLII)
and
Boudreau v. McGraw
,
2015 NBBR 6
.  Both cases involved
publications on Facebook that the plaintiff was a pedophile, as well as other
allegations.  The general damages awarded were $35,000 and $14,000,
respectively.  The Defendant argues that the defamatory comments made in both
those cases were far more serious, and that damages in this case should only be
in the sum of $2,500.  The Defendant also reminds the Court that, unlike in
those cases, the Plaintiff was not actually named in this case.

[
140
]

Interestingly,
neither party
cited
Mueller v Livingstone
, supra, a decision from
just last year where the defendant posted on Facebook that the plaintiff was a
thief – which is effectively the same allegation as in the present case.  In
that case, where the defendant appears to have acted out of frustration due to
a financial dispute over a contract, Justice Clendening of this Court awarded
$2,500 in general damages, writing:

[30]
In
Jones
, supra, Justice Morrison

referenced
Hill
v Church of Scientology
,
1995 CanLII 59 (SCC)
,
[1995] 2
SCR 1130
, and stated that the trier of fact should take into consideration all
the circumstances, including:

1.   The conduct of the plaintiff, his
position and standing;

2.   The nature of the libel;

3.   The mode and extent of
publication;

4.   The absence or refusal of any
retraction or apology; and

5.   The whole of the defendant’s conduct from the time
when the libel was published down to the very moment of the verdict.

[31]      Pursuant to compensatory damages, counsel for
Ms. Mueller is asking the court for general damages of an award between
$25,000.00 and $50,000.00.  In my view, this is excessive.  Even though Mr.
Livingstone was not justified in making his comment, Ms. Mueller did aggravate
his stress of not being paid by some of the comments she made to him.  She also
told him that she had drafted a cheque and was sending it to him, which was not
true, and she also agreed that she would accept making partial payments for
three months in October to December of 2014.  Again, this did not happen.  Mr.
Livingstone’s frustration did not, however, justify him in making the remark he
did about “this is theft”.

[32]      In considering the circumstances as set out
in
Jones
,
supra, and considering that damages are presumed, I find that a fair award for
general damages would be $2,500.00.

[
141
]

In
the present case, it cannot be ignored that the Plaintiff was not named in the
Facebook post, nor that the posting was removed the very next day.  Taking into
consideration all of the circumstances of this case, including Mr. Hawkins’
status as a leader within the business and philanthropic communities in this
province, and considering the cases referred by counsel for the Plaintiff and
for the Defendant, I feel that an award of $7,500 is reasonable in the
circumstances.  Such an award takes into account the Plaintiff’s own conduct,
which I believe led Mr. Jamieson to become extremely frustrated.  While I am in
no way condoning the defamatory posts, I do consider that Mr. Hawkins’ refusal
to honour the agreement to share profits equitably led to the dispute and,
ultimately, led Mr. Jamieson to lash out as he did.

AGGRAVATED AND PUNITIVE DAMAGES

[
142
]

Mr.
Hawkins seeks aggravated and punitive damages and argues that the total damages
in this case should be set at the financial cap for claims brought pursuant to
Rule 79, i.e. $75,000.  He argues that Mr. Jamieson sent threatening and
intimidating emails to him and attempted to coerce or “extort” him into sharing
the company’s net profits.  He argues that Mr. Jamieson’s conduct was
high-handed, oppressive and malicious.

[
143
]

In
the
Jones
case, supra, Justice Morrison had this to say regarding
the availability of aggravated and punitive damages in the context of a
defamation action:

(b)  Aggravated Damages

107.                 The plaintiff has claimed aggravated
damages.  These damages are awarded in circumstances where the defendant’s
conduct has been particularly highhanded, oppressive or malicious.  A
precondition to the award of aggravated damages is a finding that the
defendants were motivated by malice and that the malice increased the injury to
the plaintiff either through wider publication or increasing the mental
distress and humiliation of the plaintiff (
Hill v. Church of Scientology

at paragraph
189-190
).  While I have concluded that the defendants were
motivated by malice in publishing the Board Letter as they did, I cannot see
how the malice increased the distress of the plaintiff.  Despite the malicious
motivation, publication remained very limited.  Accordingly, the plaintiff’s
claim for aggravated damages is refused.

(c)  Punitive Damages

108.                 Punitive damages are the exception
rather than the rule and may be imposed where the defendant’s conduct has been
highhanded, and where the award of general damages is not sufficient to punish
or deter the egregious conduct (
Whiten v. Pilot Insurance Co
.,
2002 SCC
18 (CanLII)
,
[2002] 1 S.C.R. 595
at paragraph
94
).  The threshold issue is
whether the defendant’s conduct is so outrageous that punitive damages are
rationally required for the purposes of deterrence, denunciation and
retribution (
Delphinium Ltée. v. 512842 N.B. Inc.

(2008),
2008 NBCA 56
(CanLII)
,
333 N.B.R. (2d) 291
at paragraph
50
).  […]

[
144
]

I
am not convinced that this case is one where the award of aggravated or
punitive damages is warranted.

[
145
]

Mr.
Hawkins argues that Mr. Jamieson made the Facebook post in order to “extort” him.
I am not convinced of that, based on the evidence before me.  Mr. Jamieson’s
evidence is that the post came from a place of extreme frustration which
resulted from the financial pressures he experienced after Mr. Hawkins refused
to share XYZ’s profits.  Mr. Jamieson was not cross-examined and there is
absolutely no evidence to substantiate any other finding.

[
146
]

Further,
Mr. Hawkins’ assertion that Mr. Jamieson sent “threatening” emails to him is
not made out.  While the tone of the emails was at times aggressive and perhaps
rude, I did not identify any communications which could be described as
legitimately threatening, nor am I satisfied that Mr. Jamieson acted out of
malice.

[
147
]

Finally,
I am not satisfied that an award of aggravated or punitive damages is needed in
order to either adequately compensate Mr. Hawkins for added distress in
relation to the defamation, nor to create added deterrence as against Mr.
Jamieson.

COUNTERCLAIM

[
148
]

I
now turn to Mr. Jamieson’s counterclaim. He seeks upwards of $60,000,
representing:

a.

His
share of the Alma Club membership;

b.

His
share of the additional corporate donations made in the latter part of 2016;

c.

The
$10,000 purchase price for his shares, which was never paid by Mr. Hawkins; and

d.

The
$40,000 (estimate) in profits that he was entitled to share from XYZ.

[
149
]

At
the hearing, the Court was advised that Mr. Jamieson was dropping the claim for
the payment of the shares in XYZ which were purchased by Mr. Hawkins and Ms.
Bell-Hawkins.  Apparently, the parties were able to agree on a resolution of
that figure.

[
150
]

As
for the share of the Alma Club membership and the additional corporate
donations, I am not prepared to consider those amounts, as I have already found
that these were legitimate expenses incurred by XYZ.  Those expenses, though
perhaps irregular, were not concealed by Mr. Hawkins and the evidence suggests
that these issues arose due to Mr. Jamieson’s utter failure to act as an
engaged shareholder.  Further, Mr. Jamieson had recourse to address those
expenses as a shareholder in accordance with the
Business Corporations
Act
, S.N.B. 1981, c.B-9.1, s. 166 – the so-called “oppression remedy.”
He did not take any action with respect to those expenditures.

[
151
]

As
a result, the only claim which requires further consideration is Mr. Jamieson’s
claim for 50% of the accounts receivable, in the amount of approximately
$40,000.

[
152
]

During
argument, counsel for Mr. Hawkins argued that, even if the agreement to share
the profits survived the Buy-Sell Agreement, Mr. Jamieson has sued the wrong
party – his counterclaim is against Mr. Hawkins, another shareholder; whereas
any claim for a share of profits should have been directed at the company.  As
a shareholder, he argues, Mr. Jamieson’s claim is against XYZ, and not against
David Hawkins.  Mr. Hawkins argues that the claim cannot pierce the corporate
veil.

[
153
]

For
his part, Mr. Jamieson argues that the issue is one of semantics, as Mr.
Hawkins is the directing mind of XYZ and he is the person who has refused to
share the profits.  Further and in the alternative, Mr. Jamieson argues that
the corporate veil can and should be pierced in this case.

[
154
]

The
leading case in New Brunswick respecting the lifting or piercing of the
corporate veil remains
Estate of Michael Burke and 1021256 Ontario Inc.
v. Royal & Sun Alliance Insurance Company of Canada
,
2011 NBCA 98
(CanLII)
, a decision written by former Chief Justice Drapeau.  He wrote:

[60]      It has been hornbook law for quite some time
that a corporation is a legal entity distinct from its shareholders (see the
oft-cited
Salomon v. Salomon & Co.
,
[1897] A.C. 22
at pages 53-54
(H.L.)
). Courts will only very exceptionally disregard the separate legal
personality of a corporate entity. In
Transamerica Life Insurance Co. of
Canada v. Canada Life Assurance Co.
,
1996 CanLII 7979 (ON SC)
,
[1996] O.J.
No. 1568 (G.D.)
(QL)
, aff’d
[1997] O.J. No. 3754 (C.A.)
(QL) at para. 21
,
Justice Sharpe rejected the view that courts may lift the corporate veil
whenever they please “on some loosely defined ‘just and equitable’ standard”.
He opined that lifting the corporate veil was only appropriate
where those in control of a corporation use it as a shield
for “fraudulent or improper conduct”
(para. 22). Though this test was
articulated in connection with the distinction between a corporation and its
subsidiary, there is no principled reason to exclude its application in the
context of a one-person corporation. See, as well, the discussion in
642947
Ontario Ltd. v. Fleischer
,
2001 CanLII 8623 (ON CA)
,
[2001] O.J. No. 4771
(C.A.)
(QL) at paras.
67-69
, per Laskin J.A.

[
155
]

In
this case, Mr. Jamieson’s claim for 50% of the receivables is, in reality, a
claim against XYZ.  Mr. Jamieson confirms this expressly at paragraph 37 of his
pre-trial brief.  It is the corporate entity, and not David Hawkins, who may
distribute the profits – typically as a dividend to the shareholders.  But they
are not Mr. Hawkins’ profits, per se.

[
156
]

Mr.
Jamieson cited
Shoppers Drug Mart Inc. v. 6470360 Canada Inc. (Energyshop
Consulting Inc./Powerhouse Energy Management Inc.),

2014 ONCA 85
(CanLII)
, where the Ontario Court of Appeal lifted the corporate veil.  In that
case, the plaintiff entered into a contract with Energyshop Consulting Inc., of
which the personal defendant, Mr. Beamish, was the sole shareholder.
Energyshop had contracted with Shoppers Drug Mart to handle paying the utility
bills for a number of its pharmacies across a number of jurisdictions.  Shoppers
Drug Mart made large financial transfers into a bank account which was
controlled by Energyshop, and those funds were then used to pay the utility
bills.  At some point, Mr. Beamish caused to be transferred more than $900,000
from that account to a separate, operating account, which was jointly held by Energyshop
and by Mr. Beamish.  Some of those funds were then used for the benefit of
Energyshop’s operations.  Shoppers Drug Mart sued both Energyshop and Mr.
Beamish for the missing funds, which they argued had been misappropriated to
the benefit of Mr. Beamish as the sole shareholder of Energyshop.  Mr. Beamish
argued that the money was used by the corporate entity, and not in his personal
capacity.  The Ontario Court of Appeal confirmed that the corporate veil should
be lifted in those circumstances.

[
157
]

Mr.
Jamieson argues that the present case is similar to the
Shoppers Drug
Mart
decision, in that Mr. Hawkins’ has unlawfully refused to share the
profits, and that as the directing mind of the company and the sole shareholder
(along with his wife), he has effectively been unjustly enriched.

[
158
]

In
my view, however, that case can be distinguished.  Firstly, Mr. Jamieson has
not pleaded unjust enrichment, nor has he pleaded that the corporate veil
should be lifted.

[
159
]

Secondly,
the conduct by the shareholder in the
Shoppers Drug Mart
case is precisely
the kind of behaviour that should attract the lifting of the corporate veil -
where those in control of a corporation use it as a shield for “fraudulent or
improper conduct.”  In the present case, I have already determined that Mr.
Hawkins disregarded Mr. Jamieson’s reasonable expectations and breached the
collateral agreement pertaining to the distribution of net profits.  But I do
not believe that Mr. Hawkins’ behaviour amounts to fraud or anything akin to
fraud.  There is a significant difference between a breach of contract and
conduct which is tantamount to misappropriation or fraud.

[
160
]

As
former Chief Justice Drapeau reminds us, the corporate veil may not be lifted at
the whim of the judge simply in order to reach a just and equitable result.  If
it could, I would have no hesitation in doing so, as I am satisfied that it
would be equitable to compensate Mr. Jamieson for his half of XYZ’s profits.  But
that is not the proper test, and the Court of Appeal reminds us that we must
resist such a temptation.

[
161
]

In
my view, the corporate veil should not be lifted in this case.

[
162
]

I
am not satisfied that Mr. Jamieson has a legitimate claim as against Mr.
Hawkins personally.

[
163
]

I
should also state that, where the evidence before the Court is that Mr.
Jamieson held his shares in XYZ through his numbered company, 621947 N.B. Inc.,
Mr. Jamieson would not personally be entitled to any claim arising from the
issuance of dividends to the shareholders of XYZ.  His numbered company should
have been the party claiming those profits, and so it would seem that Mr.
Jamieson’s claim is flawed is two respects.

[
164
]

As
a result, the counterclaim is dismissed.

DISPOSITION

[
165
]

I
find that Mr. Jamieson defamed David Hawkins in his June 21, 2017 Facebook
posting by suggesting that his business partner had stolen from the company.

[
166
]

I
find that Mr. Jamieson did not defame Mr. Hawkins by suggesting that his
business partner walked away with over $100,000 in receivables.

[
167
]

I
award Mr. Hawkins general damages in the amount of $7,500; I do not award any
amounts for aggravated or punitive damages.

[
168
]

Mr.
Jamieson’s counterclaim is denied.

[
169
]

Mr.
Hawkins claims solicitor/client costs, arguing that Mr. Jamieson’s conduct has
been reprehensible, scandalous and outrageous.  Of course, the award of costs
on a solicitor/client basis is a discretionary award reserved for rare and
exceptional cases. I am not convinced that, where Mr. Hawkins has been only
partially successful, and where his own conduct has been less-than-exemplary,
an award of solicitor/client costs is appropriate.

[
170
]

Mr.
Hawkins, having had the greater success, is nonetheless entitled to costs of
$900.00 under Rule 59, Tariff A, Scale 1.  He is further entitled to his
recoverable disbursements; however, where the Court did not give any weight to
the report of Paul Bradley, the Plaintiff shall not be entitled to any recovery
of disbursements in respect of that report.
